title: The sandals and the promise
hook: two brothers argue on a mountain, each trying to give the other a kingdom
carry: satya: rama keeps even his father's word

segments.voice: Yesterday: Bharata's journey, and your line, Bharata's love comes to give, not take. Guha and Bharadvaja questioned him; Rama never doubted him.

On Chitrakoot, two brothers have an inheritance fight that runs backward: each one is trying to give the kingdom away. Bharata reaches the hut, sees Rama in bark clothes with matted hair, and falls at his feet, unable to finish a sentence. Rama lifts him up, holds him, and asks the question Bharata has dreaded the whole road. Where is our father? Why have you left him to come here?
screen: `A FIGHT TO GIVE THINGS AWAY.` → `BHARATA AT RAMA'S FEET.` → `WHERE IS OUR FATHER?`

segments.voice: Bharata tells him. The king is dead, grieving for you. Rama falls like a cut tree. When he can stand, he goes down to the Mandakini with his brothers and Sita, and offers his father water and a ball of ingudi pulp, the forest food they've been living on. In Valmiki's telling, he says: what a person eats, their ancestors eat too. Then the arguing begins, and it goes on and on. Bharata pleads: come home, be king, I'll serve you. Counselors and priests plead. Rama's answer never changes. Our father gave his word to Kaikeyi and made a promise to me. Keeping his word is how I honor him now. Fourteen years in the forest is my part; ruling Ayodhya is yours. Bharata even threatens to sit fasting at the door of the hut until Rama gives in, and Rama gently tells him that isn't the way. Finally Bharata asks for one thing. He brings out a pair of sandals adorned with gold, and asks Rama to step into them, then give them to him. Rama does. Bharata bows to the sandals. For fourteen years, he says, these will rule. I'll live outside the city in bark and matted hair, waiting for you. And if you're not back the day after fourteen years end, I'll enter the fire. Neither brother wins the argument. Both keep their word. Notice whose promise Rama is keeping: not his own, his father's, and his father is gone. Hindus call this satya, truth, and keeping your word is one of its plainest forms. In Tulsidas's Hindi Ramayana, Dasharatha names it as the custom of Rama's family, in a line families still quote: let life go, but never the word.
screen: `WATER FOR A FATHER AT THE MANDAKINI.` · `COME HOME AND BE KING.` · `I KEEP MY FATHER'S WORD.` · `STEP INTO THESE SANDALS.` · then, large: `SATYA: LET LIFE GO, NEVER THE WORD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one promise you've made that's still open: to a parent, a friend, yourself. Don't judge it. Hold it the way Rama held his father's word, as something alive. If you pray, offer it quietly to God; if you don't, just say to yourself on each breath out: I'll keep it.
The sandals. Rama steps into a pair of gold-adorned sandals and gives them to Bharata, who will set them on the throne for fourteen years.
Your line: satya, Rama keeps even his father's word. Neither brother wins, and neither breaks a promise. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Rama's sandals, the padukas, are honored in Hindu worship and art, and Ramlila performances stage the brothers' meeting at Chitrakoot.

fork.setup: you're Rama. your brother, the priests, everyone begs you to come home and be king. the father who made the promise is dead. what do you do?
options: go home. the promise died with him.
stay. his word is still his word, and i keep it for him.
fork.reveal: Rama keeps his father's word for him. that's satya, and Bharata answers with the sandals.

original.note: Sanskrit pādukā: a sandal or wooden shoe. Rama's pādukā are still honored in temples and homes.

trapdoor: what you thought: Bharata takes the sandals as a keepsake.
what it means: he takes them to place on the throne and rule in Rama's name.
what a scholar hears: Valmiki has Bharata ask Rama to step into the sandals first, so they carry his presence, and vow fire if Rama is late.

chat.meaning: Rama kept his father's word even when his brother begged him home. Families quote Tulsidas's line on it: let life go, but never the word.

tie.story: Rama refused the throne Bharata begged him to take, to keep the promise his father had given.
tie.friend: Priya gave Nani her word first, so in her family's eyes the dinner comes before the concert.
tie.you: is there a promise you're tempted to quietly drop this week?

Mandakini.meaning: the river at Chitrakoot where Rama offers water to his father

ingudi.meaning: a forest tree; its fruit pulp was the exiles' food

Chitrakoot.meaning: the mountain where the exiles made their forest home

Kaikeyi.meaning: Bharata's mother, the queen who asked for the two boons
